items.prompt: Per L1, what actually defines "white" politics — the legitimate kind this unit covers?
choices: Influence built through mechanisms that are transparent, reciprocal, and would survive being said out loud
Influence built by whoever has the most formal authority
Any influence-building that involves being genuinely liked by coworkers
Influence that never involves any self-interest at all
items.explanation: White politics is defined by the mechanism's honesty, not by the absence of strategy or self-interest. It's influence built in ways that would keep working exactly the same if fully explained out loud — that's the actual bar, not likability or formal rank.
items.reference:
🔍 Transparent — would survive being explained
🔁 Reciprocal — a real exchange over time
🧱 Built on power-real-resource's 3 non-formal sources

Why: the definition is mechanical (would it survive being said out loud), not about likability or motive.
items.learnMore:

This unit builds directly on power-real-resource's four sources of power (formal authority, expertise, relationships, information) and focuses on the legitimate ways to build the latter three — expertise through track record, relationships through reciprocity, information through genuine attention.

items.prompt: Per L1, why does help given purely to extract a later favor undermine the trust it's trying to build?
choices: It doesn't — any help works the same regardless of motive
Because reciprocity only works if it's genuine — help given with an extraction motive reads as transactional and the trust it's meant to build doesn't form
Because favors are only valid if written down formally
Because it's illegal in most workplaces
items.explanation: L1 is explicit: reciprocity's power comes from being genuine. Help whose real purpose is extracting a later favor tends to be legible as such, which produces the opposite of durable trust — a transactional read, not goodwill.
items.reference:
🤝 Genuine help, no immediate ask
↓
💛 Felt obligation, repaid voluntarily later

Why: reciprocity is a felt, unforced sense of goodwill — it collapses the moment it's clearly aimed at extraction.
items.learnMore:
Reciprocity, the core mechanism

Consistently helping people — reviewing work, sharing context, covering for someone when it matters — builds a real, felt sense of obligation. It compounds into people being willing to back you later, but only if it's genuine.

Common mistake

Treating reciprocity as a ledger to track and call in. The moment it's run like a ledger, it stops functioning like reciprocity and starts functioning like a transaction.

items.prompt: Per L1, what actually separates "white" politics from the grayer/darker forms covered later in this track?
choices: Whether it involves any strategy or awareness of relationships at all
Whether the mechanism would still work, undamaged, if the other person fully understood exactly what was being done and why
Whether the person doing it is well-liked

items.explanation: All politics involves strategy and relationship awareness — that's not the dividing line. The line is whether the mechanism depends on concealment to work: a transparent, reciprocal mechanism survives being explained; a manipulative one doesn't.
items.reference:

❌ Needs concealment to function → not white

Why: strategy and relationship awareness exist in all politics — the test is specifically about concealment dependence.

The transparency test

A genuinely generous favor and a calculated one can look identical from the outside. The test isn't about intent alone — it's mechanical: does this specific mechanism require the other person not knowing what's happening in order to keep working?

Common mistake

Assuming "has a strategic element" is disqualifying. Nearly all effective politics has a strategic element — the disqualifier is needing concealment.
